title: The best of you
hook: the best of you learn the Qur'an and teach it: the hadith that kept a teacher in his seat
tomorrow: Theo just threw his pencil. what does a good teacher do?

segments.voice: Yesterday: even one verse, as long as it's the real one. Today, a teacher who took that seriously, and the sound he kept passing on.
screen: `EVEN ONE VERSE.` → `A TEACHER, AND A SOUND.`

segments.voice: A voice note from a grandparent, reciting something slowly so a child can repeat it. Line, pause. Line, pause. In Sahih al-Bukhari there's a teacher, Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami, who taught the Qur'an in the mosque for a long time, the report says. He knew why he stayed. He pointed to one hadith and said: that is what has kept me in this seat.
screen: `LINE, PAUSE. LINE, PAUSE.` → `A TEACHER IN THE MOSQUE.` → `WHAT KEPT HIM IN HIS SEAT?`

segments.voice: The hadith he meant, from the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ: the best of you are those who learn the Qur'an and teach it. Learn and teach, in one sentence, as one job. Listen to how it's learned. By ear. The teacher reads a line; the student repeats it; the teacher fixes a vowel, a pause, a stretched sound, and the line goes again. A child at weekend school, a new Muslim with a recording, a grandmother with a grandson on her lap: the sound moves from one voice into another. That's why learn and teach sit so close. You can't teach a line you haven't learned, and a line you've taught is a line you end up knowing better. Tradition says the first word that came to the Prophet was a command to say something out loud: iqra, read, recite. In Pickthall's words: "Read: In the name of thy Lord Who createth." A book opened with a call to voice it. So the best of you, by this hadith, isn't the loudest or the one who knows the most. It's the one who keeps the sound moving, from the voice before to the voice after.
screen: `LEARN AND TEACH: ONE JOB.` · `BY EAR: LINE, REPEAT, FIX.` · `IQRA: READ, RECITE.` · `KEEP THE SOUND MOVING.` · then, large: `LEARN AND TEACH.`

segments.voice: Say bismillah out loud, slowly, the way a teacher would for a child: bis, mil, lah. Then say it again as the child would, copying your own voice. Go back and forth a few times, teacher and student, then let it go quiet.
The best of you: in the hadith, those who learn the Qur'an and teach it. One job with two halves.
Keep it handy: learn and teach, one voice handing the sound to the next. Later, then.

screen: `DAY 1747 COUNTS.` → `TEACHING AND PASSING IT ON · 2 OF 10.` → `TOMORROW: THEO THREW HIS PENCIL. NOW WHAT?`

howItsDone: Muslims learn Qur'an recitation by ear from a teacher, line by line, at mosques, weekend schools, at home and online; many who learn a passage go on to teach it to children or friends.

fork.setup: your eight-year-old nephew wants to learn al-Fatiha. you know it by heart, but not the formal rules of recitation. what fits today's hadith?
options: teach him what you know, by ear, line by line, and keep learning too.
wait until you've studied the rules properly; teaching now would be wrong.
send him an app; a trained reciter's voice will always beat yours.
fork.reveal: learn and teach sit in one sentence. the sound passes voice to voice, and the one teaching keeps learning.

notes: Confirm the exact Pickthall wording of 96:1.

Bukhari 5027: confirm numbering and that the narrator's remark ('that is what has made me sit in this seat') is fairly paraphrased. 'For a long time' stands in for the report's span (from the time of 'Uthman to al-Hajjaj); no years are given.
'Tradition says the first word that came to the Prophet was iqra' is framed as tradition; confirm.
Gloss calls al-Sulami 'an early teacher'; confirm or drop 'early'.
